newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Banks burned as A$ options turn ugly -dealers.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Banks burned as A$ options turn ugly -dealers.

text.p: Some banks likely took a beating on Australian dollar options Thursday after the currency sprang past long-standing resistance levels triggering panic hedging.

Dealers, who asked not to be named, said months of range trading by the dollar and historic low volatilities had tempted more than a few banks to sell options with strikes in the US$0.8020/8050 band. They were severely discomfited, therefore, when the dollar surged through both levels today.
"They had the view the range was iron-tight and happily pocketed the premiums," said one. "Now it's all turned ugly and they face a frightening bill for hedging the exposure."
The Australian currency has held to a broad US$0.7700/8020 range since topping out at US$0.8050 in May and for much of the time a move outside the US$0.7850/7950 band was a rarity.

That long hibernation saw option volatilities decline to eight year lows and encouraged the growth of strangle options, where a call and a put is sold with the same expiry date but different strike prices in anticipation of very little movement in the dollar.
Dealers said that recently banks began to indulge in more exotic derivatives such as range binary options which are much more leveraged, and thus more risky.
A binary option pays out a fixed amount if the underlying asset, in this case the dollar, ever reaches the strike level.
"The problem is that no one could have conceived of the AUD breaking this range that had held for so long, and certainly not so quickly," said one dealer.
"That meant many had not bothered to cover their exposure and were badly caught out when the currency cleared the US$0.8020/8050 range like a steam train," he said.
Conversely the buyers of these options, who tended to be funds and corporates taking insurance against wild swings, were now well in the money, dealers said.
Estimates of the amounts involved varied wildly -- most options traders were not returning calls to the media -- but were certainly in the hundreds of millions.
The forex dealers who were not involved had nothing but sympathy for their colleagues, knowing only too well how much pressure there was to make money even when markets were quiet.
"You have to earn money to keep your job, but what do you do when there's no volatility?" complained one.
"You take risks, first small, then larger ones. These options are not the biggest, but they're up there," he said.
